medium.title: Exported service MyService has no permission protection
medium.description: Service "edu.ksu.cs.benign.MyService" is reachable by any app on the device (android:exported="true") and declares no permission. The service `edu.ksu.cs.benign.MyService` is exported but does not define an `android:permission` attribute to restrict access.
medium.impact: Any unprivileged application on the device can start this service, potentially triggering privileged internal logic.
medium.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

reasons: The finding does not demonstrate a concrete gain or specific sensitive action that can be triggered by calling this service.

medium.title: Permission check reads the app's own identity, not the caller's
medium.description: checkPermission() reads Binder.getCallingPid() in onStartCommand(), outside any binder call, so it checks this app's own permissions rather than those of whoever started the component. The service attempts to verify the caller's identity in `onStartCommand` using `Binder.getCallingUid()`. Because `onStartCommand` is invoked by the system process, `getCallingUid()` returns the system UID rather than the UID of the originating application.
medium.impact: This allows any application to bypass the intended permission check and trigger the internal flow that starts `SensitiveActivity` with a 'SUCCESS' status.

lines: public int onStartCommand(android.content.Intent intent, int flags, int startId) {
android.util.Log.d("MyService", "Calling PID = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingPid() + " Calling UID  = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingUid());
lines_html: public class MyService extends android.app.Service {
public int onStartCommand(android.content.Intent intent, int flags, int startId) {
android.util.Log.d("MyService", "Calling PID = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingPid() + " Calling UID = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingUid());
if (checkPermission("santos.benign.permission", android.os.Binder.getCallingPid(), android.os.Binder.getCallingUid()) == 0) {
android.util.Log.d("MyService", "Service Started");
android.content.Intent activityIntent = new android.content.Intent(this, (java.lang.Class<?>) edu.ksu.cs.benign.SensitiveActivity.class);
activityIntent.addFlags(268435456);
activityIntent.putExtra("status_msg", "SUCCESS");

medium.recommendation: Guard the component with android:permission in the manifest; check a caller's permission with checkCallingPermission() only inside a binder call.

low.title: Custom permission permission is weakly protected
low.description: Custom permission "santos.benign.permission" uses protectionLevel="normal": any installed app that asks for it in its manifest is granted it at install, without the user being asked. The custom permission `santos.benign.permission` is declared without a `protectionLevel`, which defaults to `normal`.
low.impact: Any application can grant itself this permission simply by declaring it in its manifest, making the permission check effectively useless.
low.recommendation: Use protectionLevel="signature" for permissions guarding internal components.

reasons: The finding does not specify what sensitive action or data is protected by this permission.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Lack of certificate pinning is a hardening gap that only becomes a vulnerability when paired with a finding showing sensitive data on an unpinned channel.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
This is documented platform behavior that only creates a vulnerability when a specific component is implicitly exported and reachable.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 permits cleartext traffic by default
info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in. The app targets Android API level 27, which permits cleartext (HTTP) traffic by default. No network security configuration is present to restrict this behavior.
info.impact: Sensitive data transmitted over HTTP may be intercepted via man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
It identifies a configuration that allows HTTP but does not demonstrate any actual cleartext transmission.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The app does not specify a unique taskAffinity for its activities and targets an older SDK, making it susceptible to task hijacking on Android 10 and lower.
info.impact: A malicious app with the same taskAffinity can overlay its own activities on top of the app's screens, including SensitiveActivity, to steal credentials or mislead the user.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
